source_refs.note: Topic 11.10.1, printed pages 266-268, with the printed structures as drawings.

blocks.text: The structural isomerism is not confined to hydrocarbons only. In fact, all classes of organic compounds and their derivatives show the phenomenon of structural isomerism. The structural isomerism arises due to the difference in the arrangement of atoms within the molecule. The structural isomerism can be exhibited in five different ways.
This type of isomerism arises due to the difference in the nature of the carbon chain. For example, for pentane (C₅H₁₂) and butane (C₄H₁₀), the following arrangements are possible.

blocks.alt: Chain isomers: butane and 2-methylpropane (isobutane); pentane, 2-methylbutane (isopentane) and 2,2-dimethylpropane (neopentane), drawn as condensed formulae with the branches below or above the chain.
blocks.caption: Chain isomers (original drawing after the scheme printed on p266 of the textbook).

blocks.text: This type of isomerism arises due to the difference in the position of the same functional group on the carbon chain. The arrangement of carbon atoms remains the same. For example: chloropropane and butene (C₄H₈) can have two positional isomers.

blocks.alt: Position isomers: CH3-CH2-CH2-Cl, 1-chloropropane, and CH3-CH(Cl)-CH3, 2-chloropropane; CH3-CH2-CH=CH2, but-1-ene, and CH3-CH=CH-CH3, but-2-ene.
blocks.caption: Position isomers (original drawing after the scheme printed on p267 of the textbook).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints but-2-ene as CH3-CH-CH=CH3; it is CH3-CH=CH-CH3, as drawn above.

The compounds having the same molecular formula but different functional groups are said to exhibit functional group isomerism. For example, thereare two compounds having the same molecular formula C₂H₆O, but different arrangement of atoms.

blocks.alt: Functional group isomers of C2H6O: H3C-O-CH3, methoxy methane, and H3C-CH2-OH, ethanol.
blocks.caption: Functional group isomers (original drawing after the scheme printed on p267 of the textbook).

blocks.text: This type of isomerism arises due to the unequal distribution of carbon atoms on either side of the functional group. Such compounds belong to the same homologous series. For example, diethyl ether and methoxy methane.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Diethyl ether (C₄H₁₀O) and methoxy methane (C₂H₆O) do not have the same molecular formula, so they are not metamers. The printed example pair is ethoxy ethane (diethyl ether) and methoxy propane, both C₄H₁₀O.
For a ketonic compound having the molecular formula C₅H₁₀O, the following two metamers are possible.

blocks.alt: Metamers: H3C-H2C-O-CH2-CH3, ethoxy ethane, and H3C-O-CH2-CH2-CH3, methoxy propane; H3C-H2C-C(=O)-CH2-CH3, 3-pentanone, and H3C-C(=O)-CH2-CH2-CH3, 2-pentanone, with the C=O drawn upwards.
blocks.caption: Metamers (original drawing after the scheme printed on p267 of the textbook).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book names 3-pentanone '3-Pentanonone'; the correct name is 3-pentanone.

This type of isomerism arises due to shifting of proton from one atom to another in the same molecule. This is commonly seen in amino acids. They exist as zwitterions which are formed when a proton is shifted from the carboxylic acid end of amino acid molecule to the amine group.

blocks.alt: Amino acid R-C(H)(COOH)-NH2, with a curly arrow from the lone pair on N to the H of COOH, in equilibrium with the zwitterion R-C(H)(COO-)-NH3+.
blocks.caption: Tautomerism: amino acid and zwitterion (original drawing after the scheme printed on p267 of the textbook).

blocks.text: Stereoisomers are such compounds which possess the same structural formula, but differ with respect to the positions of the identical groups in space. It is part of class 12 syllabus and will be covered there.
